analysis.one_liner: Imposes rising emissions fees on large data centers and crypto mines, spending the money to lower household electric bills and build clean power.
analysis.headline: Introduced in April 2025 with two Democratic sponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and has had no further action in the Congress, which runs through January 2027.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would charge large data centers and cryptocurrency mining facilities — anything using more than 100 kilowatts of computing power — a fee for the carbon emissions from the electricity they use, whether drawn from the grid or generated on-site. The fee starts at $20 per metric ton of emissions above a regional baseline, and the baseline tightens 11% a year until it reaches zero in 2035, meaning the fee grows over time. Utilities serving these facilities would be barred from passing the fee on to regular customers, and the collected money would fund residential electricity rebates (25%), zero-carbon power and long-duration storage projects (70%), and program administration (3%). The bill would also force public disclosure of how much power these facilities use and from what sources.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary electricity customers are the main intended beneficiaries: the bill's findings note data centers are projected to use up to 12% of U.S. electricity by 2028, often reviving retired fossil plants and straining local grids, and the bill sends a quarter of collected fees to grants for lowering residential electric bills. The pass-through ban protects non-data-center utility customers from paying the fee. Communities near mining and data center operations would get cleaner air as facilities shift off fossil power, and the zero-carbon generation and long-duration storage industries would gain a large dedicated funding stream (70% of fees).

how_it_helps.text: Sends 25% of collected fees to grants for states, tribes, municipalities, and utilities to lower residential electricity costs, directly offsetting rate pressure from growing data center demand.
Bars electric utilities from recouping the emissions fee by raising rates or fees on any customer that is not a covered facility, with a penalty of twice the amount recouped for violators.
Funds zero-carbon electricity generation and long-duration energy storage with 70% of fee revenue, aimed at adding clean power rather than pushing data centers onto existing fossil supply.

Requires annual public reporting of each facility's power consumption and emissions intensity, addressing what the bill's findings call a lack of transparency about the energy sources behind cryptomining and data centers.

analysis.who_pays: Owners of large data centers and cryptomining facilities pay the fees for emissions above the regional baseline, including for power generated behind their own meters; utilities serving them are assessed the grid-side fee and must absorb it rather than pass it on. Facilities run entirely on zero-carbon power are exempt. Costs could also surface indirectly in prices for cloud computing, AI services, and cryptocurrency, and fossil plants brought back online to power mining would lose the economics that revived them.

drawbacks.text: The fee only applies to emissions above a regional baseline, so data centers located in already-clean grid regions pay nothing even as their sheer electricity demand still raises consumption and can push up rates for everyone else.
Only facilities over 100 kilowatts of installed computing power are covered, leaving smaller operations unregulated.

Fee costs could be passed to consumers indirectly through higher prices for cloud services, artificial intelligence tools, and cryptocurrency, and critics of such measures argue energy-hungry operations could simply move to countries without emissions fees.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real, growing consumer cost — data center and cryptomining electricity demand that is projected to reach up to 12% of U.S. electricity use by 2028 and is pulling retired fossil plants back online — and channels the money back to households. Its main design weakness is that the fee keys off regional grid emissions intensity rather than total electricity demand, so facilities in clean-grid regions escape the fee even while their load contributes to rate increases and the need for new generation. The pass-through ban is the strongest consumer protection, since it keeps the fee from landing on regular utility customers' bills.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in April 2025, and nothing has happened to it since — no hearing, no markup, no vote — while the current Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, joined by Sen. John Fetterman, introduced the Clean Cloud Act of 2025 on April 10, 2025.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
The full action history shows no further activity after the referral — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action.

The bill would establish an emissions standard and fee system for large data centers and cryptomining facilities, and appropriate the collected fees for zero-carbon generation, long-duration energy storage, and grants to lower residential electricity costs.
The current Congress runs through January 3, 2027, so the bill technically remains alive.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data center and cryptomining companies, which face no new emissions fees, and electric utilities, which face no new reporting or fee obligations as long as the bill sits untouched in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data center and cryptomining operators, for now

for.name: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Clean Cloud Act of 2025 on April 10, 2025 and is its lead sponsor.

for.name: Sen. John Fetterman
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's sole cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Accepted the referral on the day of introduction and has taken no further action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the session so far.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors are Democrats and no Republican has joined; with no vote and no recorded statements, there is no record of who else supports or opposes it.

industries.note: The bill's findings describe proof-of-work mining as energy-intensive by design and note that retired fossil plants are being brought back online to power it. The facilities would pay fees on above-baseline emissions, including from on-site generation, and would face public disclosure of their power sources.

industries.industry: Large data center and cloud/AI operators
industries.note: Operators of large data centers would pay fees on emissions above the regional baseline unless their power is entirely zero-carbon, and strict rules would limit counting paper renewable contracts toward that exemption. Their interest in cheap, abundant power — often fossil-backed — runs against residential ratepayers' interest, though some costs could surface in cloud and AI service prices.

Utilities would be assessed fees for serving covered facilities and would face new reporting requirements, but are barred from passing the fee on to non-data-center customers. They could also benefit from the fee revenue funding clean power grants and residential cost relief.

industries.industry: Zero-carbon generation and long-duration energy storage
industries.note: 70% of collected fees would fund grants, rebates, advanced market commitments, and low-interest loans for firm zero-carbon generation and 10-plus-hour storage, and data centers would need genuinely new clean power to avoid fees.

The bill targets the practice of reviving retired fossil plants to power mining and data centers; plants brought back for that purpose would generate fee liabilities for the utilities serving covered facilities, eroding the economics that revived them.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has one sponsor and one cosponsor, no Republican support, and no committee activity since its April 2025 referral to the Republican-led Environment and Public Works Committee. Bills at this stage with this level of support typically never receive a hearing or markup and expire at the end of the Congress on January 3, 2027.
